headline: Snake on a Swing Set: Three-Year-Old Bitten in Livingston Parish, Cottonmouth Found on Baton Rouge Patio
summary: A 3-year-old girl is recovering after a venomous snake bit her on a swing set in Walker, and a Baton Rouge woman found a cottonmouth on her patio as snake sightings rise with cooler mornings.
body:
I'm Philip Massouh, and this is SnakeNews. Tonight, the swing set is a strike zone, the backyard patio is a coiled threat, and the cooler morning air is waking up every legless menace in Louisiana. A three-year-old girl from Livingston Parish is out of the hospital after a venomous snake bit her while she played on her swing set this week. We are not talking about a faraway jungle. We are talking about Walker, Louisiana, where the grass is green, the kids are outside, and the snakes are moving.

According to family members who spoke with WBRZ, the child came running inside in tears after the bite. Her grandmother, Becca Young-kin, described the moment. "We heard her cry, she said the big long thing bit her, and you could tell there were bite marks from a snake," Young-kin recalled. The little girl was rushed to the hospital, where doctors gave her anti-venom. She has since been released. That is the good news. The terrifying news is that her family is not alone.

Hilton Cole at East Baton Rouge Parish Animal Control says an increase in snake sightings across the area is tied to cooler temperatures in the morning. When the air cools off, snakes start moving, and that means they end up in yards, on patios, and around swing sets. In Baton Rouge, Brandy Parsons found a cottonmouth coiled up on her patio this week after her dog discovered it. Her backyard oasis went from relaxing to rattled. "We are kind of scared to walk outside, have to check everything," Parsons said. She took her dog to the vet after it started acting strangely. Blood tests showed the dog was fine, but the shock is still there. Parsons says she does not usually see snakes in her part of Baton Rouge.

The families have a simple warning for everyone. Parsons put it plainly: "In the grass, make sure you are looking before you walk." Young-kin added that parents should pay attention to where their children are playing and check the area first, because this bite happened on a swing set, a place that should be safe. Doctors advise that after a snakebite, people should watch for shortness of breath, pain at the bite site, swelling, and other symptoms. If someone can safely take a picture of the snake, it may help doctors identify the species, but the priority is getting to a hospital.

Now it is time for the SnakeNews Safety Desk. I checked in with our own overnight producer, Connie Strictor, who keeps a laminated snakebite card taped to the wall of the control room. Connie says the advice is the same in Louisiana, California, and everywhere else. If someone is bitten, call 911 immediately. Keep the person calm and as still as possible. Keep the bitten arm or leg immobilized, and try to keep it at or below the level of the heart. Remove any rings, watches, or tight clothing before swelling starts. Do not apply a tourniquet. Do not cut the wound. Do not try to suck out the venom. Those movie moves make things worse. The only cure for venom is anti-venom in a hospital, so get there fast. If you can snap a photo from a safe distance without chasing the snake, do it, but do not risk another bite.

Now, about that cottonmouth in Baton Rouge. A cottonmouth, also called a water moccasin, is a venomous snake that lives in the southeastern United States, including Louisiana. It usually prefers swamps, marshes, ponds, creeks, and slow-moving water, but as we saw this week, it will absolutely curl up on a patio if that patio is warm or if it is on the move. The child in Walker was bitten by a venomous snake, and while this report does not identify the exact species in that case, the region is home to more than one kind of venomous snake, so the warning applies across the board. What matters is that the girl got anti-venom and is now out of the hospital.

And now, the Santa Monica check-in, because I know you are worried about me. I'm Philip Massouh, and I am still right here in Santa Monica. No cottonmouths under the anchor desk. No serpents in the teleprompter. No fangs in my coffee cup. My dad and uncle will tell you the snakes are coming for me, and I checked the crawlspace, the backyard, the parking lot, and even the little patch of ice plant by the news van. I am fine. The only thing biting in Santa Monica tonight is the marine layer, and I have a jacket for that.

For the families in Walker and Baton Rouge, keep your eyes open. Check the swing set before the kids climb on. Check the patio before the dog goes out. Look down before you step into the grass. This is SnakeNews, reminding you that a long thing with no legs can ruin a whole afternoon. For SnakeNews, I'm Philip Massouh. Stay alert, stay safe, and if you see a big long thing, back away and call someone who knows snakes. If it bites, call 911 first.
